questions.q: A character says, 'I'm hurt because you never listened to me.' What's the diagnosis?
choices: On-the-nose dialogue: the feeling is stated, leaving nothing to play
questions.explain: Give her a reason not to say it, and something else to talk about.

questions.q: In Annie Hall, Alvy and Annie chat about photography while subtitles show their real anxieties. What is the scene exposing?
questions.explain: Allen makes the hidden layer visible as a joke.

questions.q: You cover the names on a page of your script and can't tell who's speaking. What's missing?
questions.explain: Each character needs their own words, rhythms and habits.

questions.q: What does McKee's subtitle 'The Art of Verbal Action' imply?
choices: Dialogue should be cut wherever possible
Every line is something a character does to someone, not just information
questions.explain: Dialogue is action, an idea that runs from Stanislavski through Mamet to McKee.

questions.q: Which filmmaker built a sound system with separate tracks and radio microphones so several conversations could overlap?
questions.explain: Altman, on California Split and Nashville. Hawks used rapid overlap earlier, but performed it live.

questions.q: In On the Waterfront's taxi scene, why does Terry's 'contender' speech work as dramatic dialogue?
choices: It's an action: an accusation under pressure that changes what Charley does
It explains Terry's backstory to the audience
questions.explain: It's a crisis speech that does something: Charley lets him go.

questions.q: A source tells you, 'Me and him was gonna, uh, we was gonna fix it.' What's the most defensible approach?
choices: Fix the grammar silently; Masson says it's legal
Fix it only if the speaker is a public official
Quote exactly, or paraphrase, and treat all sources by the same standard
Invent a cleaner quote with the same meaning
questions.explain: Many style guides forbid altering quotes; Masson is a legal floor, and tidying only some people's speech is unfair.

questions.q: In Pinter's plays, what do the marked pauses and silences usually signal?
choices: The actor has forgotten a line
A moment for the audience to laugh
Moments of pressure, often where power shifts
questions.explain: What isn't said can be the loudest thing in the room.

ideas: Which approach treats every line as a move one character makes against another?
Which approach finds the real scene in what characters avoid saying?
Which approach lets several conversations run over each other so the scene feels eavesdropped?
Which approach writes silence into the script as a measured event?
